<reason>A's core strategic move — pointing out that under the status quo switch, winter already runs on standard time, so B's entire opening (dark bus stops, winter commuters) was actually an argument against permanent summer time, a position nobody in the room held — landed early and was never fully neutralized by B. B pivoted in later rounds to the transition-harm argument (health spikes from the biannual jolt), which is a real and legitimate point, but A met it with a plausible mechanism (sleep debt is anticipatable, autumn returns the hour, spikes are concentrated timing shifts among already at-risk people) and, crucially, B never adequately answered A's recurring, specific claim that permanent standard time dumps daylight on empty pre-dawn streets while stripping it from the crowded evening commute and after-school hours. That asymmetry in unanswered ground, plus A's sharper, more concrete rebuttals and cleaner closing framing (the thermostat analogy), gives A the more convincing path to victory. B asked sharp pressure questions and answered A's competently in proper A1/A2 format, but its case never fully recovered from the early strategic misfire of attacking a position CON didn't hold, and its closing largely repeated prior framing rather than closing the evening-safety gap. Execution-wise, A was clipped twice for length versus B's one clipping, a minor cost, but the substantive core of A's arguments was already delivered before each cutoff.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's [A2.1]/[A1.1] move showing that B's opening evidence about dark winter mornings is already satisfied by the existing switch (winter runs on standard time), which reframes the entire debate onto summer evening light — ground B never fully answered.</best_rebuttal>
